data.content:
#SCENE
Composition is extremely important to the overall cinematic quality of a shot. If you only describe a scene directly to AI, it may not give you a strong or well-controlled composition. My approach is to find frames from classic films in the flick.art library and then use Nano Banana to modify the environment. It’s important to clearly state in your prompt that the composition, camera angle, focal length, and overall framing should remain unchanged, while only the environment is replaced with the one you need. You can take a closer look at my prompt to see how I kept the result closely aligned with the feel of the original frame.

Replace the bamboo pole with a thin weather-beaten wooden marker pole, long and slightly curved, eroded by wind and snow.

data.content:
#CHARACTER
In most cases, we’ll want to create standard character reference images that include front, three-quarter, and side views of both the face and the full body. During production, though, you may also need additional angles or close-up references for specific shots. For example, later in my process I needed a full back view. If I had relied only on the original three-view turnaround, there was a good chance the model would generate a side view instead of a true back-facing view. So I created an extra full-body back-view reference image specifically for that need.

#Iterating Frames
After creating the base of your starting frame, you can continuously iterate on it to refine the exact scene you have in mind. This includes adjusting elements like lighting, camera angle, time of day, and zoom to get the perfect composition. You can do this by using the **Image Edit** feature on your base frame with high-power AI models like Midjourney, Nano Banana and GPT-Image to push the realism and cinematic quality further. This stage is all about refining and experimenting until the scene matches your vision. Check these frames out and observe how the creator iterated through their frames to come up with their ideal frame. Observe how the subtle changes in these scenes can provide a huge mood difference.

#Additional Features
Some other useful features in the Flick canvas include **Archive** and **Chat**. **Archive** allows you to store nodes in the archive library, which can be accessed by clicking **Shots** on the sidebar. This is useful for clearing up your canvas while keeping nodes accessible, in case you need them later on. **Chat** is accessible on the right side of the screen. Flick's chat is capable of editing and creating images and videos for you as well as answer any questions you might have about the platform.

data.content:
#Character Design
After defining your setting, the next step is creating your characters. Focus on defining their personality, vibe, and physical traits based on their role in the story. For example, the armoured warrior carries a more confident aura compared to the other 2 characters . Once you create your character, it’s also a good idea to generate shots of different angles—such as front, back, side, and close-up shots—so you can consistently use them across future scenes. You can do this by referencing your base character shot and using on of many AI models provided by Flick to generate the different perspectives. You can also reference the prompts used for these shots to get a deeper understanding of how to produce these results.

The setting of your story is one of the most important parts of your film, helping define the mood, atmosphere, and era. A great way to create cinematic settings in the **Film** section on Flick.art is by selecting a frame from a movie and using Flick’s vast variety of high power AI models to modify the environment to match your vision. Using a film frame gives the AI a strong visual reference, leading to better results—just make sure your prompt clearly describes what you want changed.

#Creating with Blender
In these workflow examples, we can see how creators use Flick to bring their 3D Blender scenes to life. Start by uploading an image of your Blender scene to your canvas using the **Upload** feature. Once uploaded, you can reference that image to generate a pencil sketch version of your scene. For even better results, try using Flick’s **Visual Style Reference** feature to guide the sketch style and maintain consistency. After creating your sketch, you can turn it into a polished frame using the **Character Reference** feature. This allows you to replace the placeholder characters in the sketch with the custom characters you designed earlier. Once your frame is ready, generate a video from it to fully bring your scene to life.

data.content:
#Creating the Scene
After you have your ideal starting frame, you can go ahead and generate a video from that frame. Select your starting frame and click **Generate Video** in the video section of the action menu. Be sure to use a specific prompt to describe the overall progression of the scene. Some useful features for this step include **Motion Reference** and **Omni Reference**. **Motion Reference** lets you use a video as the motion source when you generate a new clip: connect a still of your subject and a driving video, then run the action to animate that subject with the reference movement. **Omni Reference** is for building a scene from multiple references—images, videos, and audio on Seedance, or element references and optional start/end frames on Kling—with a prompt that calls out those assets with @ tags. You can use these features and the regenerate feature to iterate until you get your desired scene.
